themes.label: Editorial, Textual, and Publishing Context
themes.rationale: Encompasses paratextual details, translator prefaces, acknowledgments, publication history, apparatus, index summaries, and editorial notes on text collation.

themes.label: The Nature and Definition of Justice
themes.rationale: Covers the fundamental inquiry into the definition, intrinsic worth, and traditional or sophistical views of justice in Books I-II, moving from Cephalus and Polemarchus to Thrasymachus, Glaucon, and Adeimantus.

themes.label: Founding and Architecture of the Ideal City
themes.rationale: Focuses on the genesis of the state, class division of labor, communal institutions, guardian training, and the harmony of the whole civic body across Books II-V.

themes.label: Education, Aesthetics, and Cultural Purgation
themes.rationale: Concerns the moral, musical, and physical cultivation of citizens and guardians, the critique of poets and Homer, the distinction of true lies, and the reform of medicine and law.

themes.label: Psychology, Soul Tripartition, and Personal Virtue
themes.rationale: Traces the structural analysis of the human soul into rational, spirited, and appetitive elements, psychic harmony as health, the hierarchy of pleasures, and personal virtue.

themes.label: Epistemology, Dialectic, and the Metaphysics of the Good
themes.rationale: Explores the philosopher-king ideal, the distinction between knowledge and opinion, the Sun, Line, Cave allegories, the mathematical quadrivium, dialectic, and the Idea of the Good.

themes.label: Regime Decline, Tyranny, and Eschatological Justice
themes.rationale: Examines the degeneration of regimes and souls from timocracy to tyranny, the misery of the tyrant, the mathematical interval of 729, soul immortality, and the Myth of Er.

crossEdges.rationale: Chunk 4 commentary abstracts the first stage of morality (truth-telling and paying debts) directly exemplified by Cephalus and Socrates in Chunk 19.
Thrasymachus's original dialogue claim that justice is the interest of the stronger (chunk 19) grounds the analytical formulation of the 'Might is Right' thesis in chunk 4.
Socrates' dialectical argument that arts serve only the interest of their subjects (chunk 20) supports the commentator's concept of the Analogy of the Arts (chunk 4).
Glaucon's social compact speech in chunk 22 provides the direct primary basis for the commentary summary of the social contract of the weaker in chunk 4.
The Ring of Gyges myth in chunk 22 serves as the concrete thought experiment illustrating the commentary's thesis in chunk 4.
Adeimantus's explicit demand in chunk 22 defines the central organizing question of justice in itself described in chunk 4.
The dialogue passage of the large letters in chunk 22 provides the exact methodological basis for the commentator's analysis of the state-individual analogy in chunk 5.
The dialogue deduction of specialization in chunk 22 grounds the commentary's analysis of division of labor in chunk 5.
Socrates' account of the fevered city and territorial expansion in chunk 23 directly supports the commentary analysis of the luxurious city and guardians in chunk 5.
The theological rule that God causes only good in chunk 23 provides the formal definition of the first canon analyzed in chunk 5.
The dialogue restriction on guardian mimesis in chunk 24 provides the explicit premise for the commentary summary on poetic imitation restrictions in chunk 5.
Socrates' dialogue defense of retaining only Dorian and Phrygian modes in chunk 25 directly substantiates the commentary on musical purgation in chunk 5.
The critique of Asclepius and prolonged doctoring in chunk 25 supports the commentary claim in chunk 6 regarding soul and physical training.
The dialogue conclusion that music and gymnastic harmonize reason and passion in chunk 25 grounds the commentary synthesis in chunk 6.
The Phoenician tale of metals told in chunk 26 supplies the textual definition for the commentator's discussion of the noble lie in chunk 6.
The dialogue rules banning private property and money for guardians in chunk 26 define the guardian property regulations analyzed in chunk 6.
Socrates' reply to Adeimantus regarding the statue and the whole city in chunk 27 grounds the commentary analysis of whole-state happiness in chunk 6.
The warning against musical innovation and superfluous legislation in chunk 27 directly supports the commentary thesis in chunk 6.
The identification of civic wisdom and courage in classes in chunk 27 supports the commentary's summary of the cardinal virtues in chunk 7.
The definition of state justice in chunk 28 as each class doing its own business substantiates the commentary account of justice in chunk 7.
The dialogue proof of the three parts of the soul in chunk 28 supports the commentary's tripartite soul framework in chunk 7.
The dialogue arguments for identical gymnastics and war training for women in chunk 29 ground the commentary claim on equal female roles in chunk 7.
The dialogue proposals of regulated lotteries and nurseries in chunk 29 substantiate the commentary account of communal guardian families in chunk 8.
The dialogue analogy of the wounded finger and bodily empathy in chunk 30 provides the exact imagery analyzed in chunk 8.
Socrates' primary declaration of the philosopher-king paradox in chunk 30 defines the thesis examined in chunk 8.
The proof distinguishing infallible knowledge from fallible opinion in chunk 31 directly supports the commentary discussion in chunk 8.
The narrative parable of the mutinous ship and star-gazer pilot in chunk 32 exemplifies the commentary's ship parable analysis in chunk 8.
Socrates' dialogue exposition of the Sun as offspring of the good in chunk 33 defines the Sun analogy analyzed in chunk 9.
The proportional division of the line in chunk 33 provides the primary definition for the Divided Line commentary in chunk 9.
The cave narrative with chained prisoners in chunk 35 exemplifies the commentary's analysis of the Allegory of the Cave in chunk 9.
